overview: This file concerns Japanese tonnage dues, customs formalities, and port-entry requirements, centering on the anomalous use of the U.S. Navy vessel U.S.S. Gold Star to carry privately owned commercial cargo between Japan and Guam. It combines a 1935 cross-reference concerning entry into unopened ports; a 1937 Kobe consular despatch with four documents from 1933 tracing the Gold Star dispute; State, Navy, Commerce, and Embassy correspondence that led the Navy to restrict the vessel to government cargo; and a separate inquiry concerning the S.S. Texas’s fueling stop at Yokohama. The bundle also contains an apparently misfiled fragment of a consular report on wartime aviation, shipping disruption, and anti-spy conditions in Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on entry into unopened Japanese ports
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a Japanese Embassy inquiry about American rules and charges governing entry into unopened and open ports.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Embassy asked whether ships in the United States could receive special permission to enter an unopened port, comparable to Article 98 of the Japanese Customs Law. It also requested the applicable fees and the rate of tonnage duty at an open port. The sheet directs the reader to file 611.00231/7 for the underlying note.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 196 on commercial cargo carried by the U.S.S. Gold Star
subfiles.from: Winthrop R. Scott, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Scott forwards a detailed account of the disputed carriage of commercial cargo from Japan to Guam by a U.S. Navy vessel.
subfiles.summary: Scott reports that Japan had tolerated the Gold Star’s commercial shipments without imposing normal tonnage dues, while refusing to concede that such activity was properly exempt. He warns that the issue should be regularized if government vessels are to continue carrying commercial cargo to Guam, particularly under current wartime conditions. His November 4 letter to Consul General Cameron is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Scott’s confidential letter to Cameron on the Gold Star dispute
subfiles.from: Winthrop R. Scott, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.to: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Scott reconstructs the Gold Star’s customs dispute from 1933 through 1937 and recommends either paying commercial dues or ending private shipments.
subfiles.summary: The dispute began in August 1933 when Kobe Customs sought merchant-vessel declarations and warned that tonnage dues could be imposed on privately owned cargo carried by the Gold Star. Despite Japanese objections and a reported U.S. naval prohibition, the vessel continued its semiannual carriage of private cargo through Kobe and Yokohama without paying dues. A September 1937 dispute over cement was resolved after intervention through the Embassy and Foreign Office, but the ship’s captain intended to continue carrying cargo. Scott calls the status unsatisfactory and recommends obtaining formal Japanese permission and paying ordinary dues, or instructing the vessel to carry no commercial cargo.

subfiles.title: Unsigned Kobe Customs memorandum on warships carrying merchandise
subfiles.from: Official of the Kobe Custom House
subfiles.to: Commander of the U.S.S. Gold Star
subfiles.about: Kobe Customs states that a warship loading or unloading merchandise is liable to treatment as a merchant ship and to tonnage dues.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that ships loading or discharging cargo at an open Japanese port are engaged in overseas trade and ordinarily owe tonnage dues. Warships may handle articles required for their own use but not merchandise. Customs waived the dues on this occasion by treating the cargo as ship’s stores, while warning that future commercial operations would be assessed as those of a merchant vessel.

subfiles.title: Commander Faus’s request for assistance over threatened tonnage dues
subfiles.from: W. C. Faus, commanding the U.S.S. Gold Star
subfiles.about: Faus asks the consul to determine whether Japan will impose tonnage dues on the Gold Star at Kobe or other Japanese ports.
subfiles.summary: Faus reports the unsigned memorandum left by customs official T. Inouye and asks whether its threatened charges represent a final, nationwide decision. He describes the Gold Star’s carriage of copra into Japan and coal, cement, rice, malt extract, and general merchandise to Guam, emphasizing the economic benefit to Japan from cargo, passengers, and crew spending. He argues that U.S. law provides no authority for a warship to pay tonnage dues and warns that the Governor of Guam might cease routing the vessel through Japan.

subfiles.title: Kobe Customs response on the Gold Star’s commercial cargo
subfiles.from: Tsutomu Kubotera, Director of Kobe Customs
subfiles.to: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Kubotera distinguishes the Gold Star’s immunity as a warship from the customs consequences of carrying general commercial goods.
subfiles.summary: Kobe Customs acknowledges that the Gold Star, as an American man-of-war, would not normally be subject to tonnage or other dues. Loading or discharging general commercial articles, however, amounts to foreign trade and raises obligations under Japanese customs law. Although Customs declines to assess the vessel on this occasion, Kubotera asks that it discontinue carrying substantial cargo not intended for the ship’s use.

subfiles.title: Garrels letter reporting a naval prohibition on cargo carriage
subfiles.to: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Garrels reports that the Gold Star’s commander had supposedly been instructed to obey regulations prohibiting U.S. naval vessels from transporting cargo.
subfiles.summary: Garrels refers to earlier correspondence among the Kobe Consulate, Embassy, and Consulate General concerning tonnage dues. He states that the issue had been referred to the Commander of the Asiatic Fleet. According to the information received, the Gold Star’s commanding officer was instructed to comply with naval regulations prohibiting naval vessels from transporting cargo.

subfiles.title: State Department letter requesting the Navy’s views on the Gold Star
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The State Department asks the Navy to resolve whether the Gold Star should pay commercial dues or stop carrying private cargo.
subfiles.summary: Hull transmits the Kobe despatch and summarizes Japan’s tolerance of the Gold Star’s trade without any concession that naval vessels carrying commercial cargo remain exempt from dues. He notes the conflict between the earlier report of a naval prohibition and the vessel’s continuing semiannual trade. The Department asks for the Navy’s views, observing that Scott, the ambassador, the consul general, and the naval attaché favor payment of ordinary dues or termination of private shipments.

subfiles.title: Telegram asking the Tokyo Embassy for its views
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether the Embassy was consulted about the Kobe despatch and whether it has comments before the issue is taken up with the Navy.
subfiles.summary: The telegram cites Kobe’s November 9 despatch and its enclosure concerning the Gold Star. Before consulting the Navy Department, the Department of State requests confirmation of the Embassy’s involvement and its opinion on the dispute.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram recommending dues or an end to private freight
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grew states the Embassy’s position that the Gold Star should pay commercial dues or stop carrying freight for private parties.
subfiles.summary: Replying to the Department’s December 16 telegram, Grew endorses a clear two-way resolution: payment of commercial dues or discontinuation of private freight. He adds that both the consul general and the naval attaché concur.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting verification of Japanese port-entry law
subfiles.about: The Department asks the Embassy to verify a claim that every ship stopping at Yokohama must enter and clear even when it only takes on fuel.
subfiles.summary: At the Commerce Department’s request, the telegram quotes a petition concerning the S.S. Texas. The vessel allegedly stopped at Yokohama solely to take bunker oil from its company’s bonded tank and handled no cargo. The Embassy is asked to verify whether Japanese law nevertheless required formal entry and clearance.

subfiles.title: Fragment of report on wartime conditions in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: This incomplete report describes military aviation, shipping disruption, property removal, and anti-spy intimidation in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages describe army aircraft publicly departing toward the fighting near Shanghai and an army-plane crash at Taihoku that led military authorities to remove more than 300 nearby Chinese-owned houses. Steamship service between Taiwan and Japan had been sharply reduced because vessels were commandeered for evacuation and transport duties connected with China. Rowe reports no internal disturbances but says intense anti-spy propaganda made even innocent information gathering difficult for the consulate.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram explaining Japanese tonnage and entry requirements
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grew confirms that foreign vessels entering Japanese ports for cargo, repairs, or fuel generally owe tonnage dues and must complete entry and clearance formalities.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy states that Japanese law applies tonnage dues and normal entry and clearance procedures to foreign vessels regardless of whether their purpose is cargo handling, repairs, or fueling. Exemption is confined to vessels entering because of disaster at sea or other unavoidable circumstances. The reply therefore confirms the substance of the statement concerning the S.S. Texas.

subfiles.title: Navy acknowledgment pending the Governor of Guam’s advice
subfiles.about: The Navy acknowledges the State Department’s Gold Star inquiry and postpones its opinion until the Governor of Guam responds.
subfiles.summary: Leahy states that the Department of State’s letter and enclosures are being sent to the Governor of Guam by Clipper airmail. The Navy will provide its views on the commercial-cargo problem after receiving the governor’s recommendations.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department request concerning the S.S. Texas
subfiles.from: J. M. Johnson, Assistant Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Commerce asks State to determine whether Japanese law required the S.S. Texas to enter and clear at Yokohama during a fueling-only stop.
subfiles.summary: Johnson quotes a petition submitted to the Bureau of Marine Inspection and Navigation. The petition claims that the S.S. Texas neither loaded nor discharged cargo at Yokohama but stopped only for bunker oil from a bonded company tank. Commerce requests an early verification of the asserted Japanese legal requirement so the Bureau can decide the petition.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on Japanese law governing fueling stops
subfiles.from: Hugh R. Wilson, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Daniel C. Roper, Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: State forwards the Tokyo Embassy’s confirmation that fueling-only calls are ordinarily subject to Japanese tonnage dues and port formalities.
subfiles.summary: Wilson quotes the Embassy’s December 23 telegram in response to Commerce’s inquiry about the S.S. Texas. Foreign vessels visiting Japanese ports for cargo, repairs, or fueling must pay tonnage dues and enter and clear in the normal manner. Only disaster at sea or comparable unavoidable circumstances create an exemption.

subfiles.title: Navy decision restricting the Gold Star to government cargo
subfiles.from: William D. Leahy, Acting Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The Navy announces that the Gold Star will carry only government cargo between Guam and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Navy identifies two possible solutions: cease handling commercial cargo in Japan or pay tonnage dues and prorate them among Guam merchants. Although General Order No. 6 contemplated compliance with merchant-vessel consular regulations when naval vessels carried commercial cargo, paying dues risked confusing the Gold Star’s public-vessel status. The Navy therefore directed the Governor of Guam by radio on February 2 to limit the vessel to government cargo.

subfiles.title: Instruction to notify Japanese consulates of the Navy’s decision
subfiles.about: The Department transmits the Navy’s decision and instructs the Embassy to inform American consular offices in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter reviews the December telegram exchange concerning private commercial cargo carried by the Gold Star. It encloses the Navy’s February 4 decision that the ship will transport only government cargo between Guam and Japan. The Embassy is directed to circulate that decision to consular offices throughout Japan.

interest: The file is especially useful for studying the uncertain boundary between warship immunity and commercial activity: Japanese officials did not deny the Gold Star’s public-vessel status, but argued that carrying private merchandise brought it within ordinary customs rules. The correspondence also illuminates Guam’s dependence on Japanese supplies, the informal accommodations used to sustain that trade, and the interdepartmental process by which State, Navy, Commerce, and overseas posts converted a recurring local dispute into a formal cargo restriction. The 1933 enclosures provide unusually detailed evidence about commodities, tonnages, passenger traffic, and officials’ competing legal arguments, while the stray Taiwan fragment offers a revealing snapshot of wartime mobilization and anti-spy anxiety.
